statement: Proxima Centauri is gravitationally bound to the Alpha Centauri AB pair (this record is component A) with a high degree of confidence; Kervella et al. 2017 find an orbital period of about 550,000 years and an eccentricity of 0.50 (+0.08, -0.09).

source.label: Kervella, Thevenin & Lovis 2017, Proxima's orbit around Alpha Centauri (arXiv:1611.03495) [retrieved 2026-11-13]

statement: Proxima Centauri is gravitationally bound to the Alpha Centauri AB pair (this record is component B) with a high degree of confidence; Kervella et al. 2017 find an orbital period of about 550,000 years and an eccentricity of 0.50 (+0.08, -0.09).

source.label: Kervella, Thevenin & Lovis 2017, Proxima's orbit around Alpha Centauri (arXiv:1611.03495) [retrieved 2026-11-13]

statement: Alpha Centauri A and B are the two components of one binary, for which Pourbaix & Boffin 2016 derive a full three-dimensional orbit and masses of 1.13 and 0.97 solar masses.

source.label: Pourbaix & Boffin 2016, Parallax and masses of alpha Centauri revisited (arXiv:1601.01636) [retrieved 2026-11-13]

statement: The Sun lies inside the Milky Way, about 8178 pc from the Galactic Centre in the atlas model (GRAVITY Collaboration 2019 for the distance; Bland-Hawthorn & Gerhard 2016 for the Galaxy structure).

source.label: GRAVITY Collaboration 2019, A geometric distance measurement to the Galactic Center black hole with 0.3% uncertainty (arXiv:1904.05721) [retrieved 2026-11-13]; structure: Bland-Hawthorn & Gerhard 2016, The Galaxy in Context (arXiv:1602.07702), used by the atlas Milky Way model [retrieved 2026-11-13]

statement: Sgr A*, a massive black hole, sits at the Galactic Centre of the Milky Way; the star S2 orbits it (GRAVITY Collaboration 2019) and the radio source is argued to be a massive black hole of about 4.4 million solar masses (Genzel et al. 2010).

source.label: GRAVITY Collaboration 2019, A geometric distance measurement to the Galactic Center black hole with 0.3% uncertainty (arXiv:1904.05721) [retrieved 2026-11-13]; Genzel, Eisenhauer & Gillessen 2010, The Galactic Center Massive Black Hole and Nuclear Star Cluster (arXiv:1006.0064) [retrieved 2026-11-13]
